description:
FOUND s496a (Opus, 2026-09-26), member 3 of #2060.

`\X` is now perl's LEGACY approximation `(?>\r\n|\P{M}\p{M}*|\p{M}+)` (a base character with its combining marks), which the Unicode property support (#2060) made possible.  It is still NOT UAX #29 extended grapheme clusters, and these differ from perl 5.40.3:

    sub m1 { ($_[0] =~ $_[1]) ? 1 : 0 }
    print m1("\x{1F1E6}\x{1F1E8}", qr/^\X$/), " ",                  # regional-indicator PAIR
          scalar(() = "\x{1100}\x{1161}" =~ /\X/g), " ",            # Hangul L + V
          scalar(() = "\x{1F468}\x{200D}\x{1F469}" =~ /\X/g), "\n"; # emoji ZWJ sequence
  perl:        1 1 1
  PCL s496a:   0 2 3

A faithful \X needs the Grapheme_Cluster_Break property (gcb=, NOT generated by tools/rebuild-uniprops today -- it is in the "dies" list) plus the UAX #29 rules GB3-GB13 (Extend, SpacingMark, Prepend, L/V/T/LV/LVT, ZWJ + Extended_Pictographic, RI pairs).  cl-ppcre has no grapheme primitive, so it is either a pattern built from gcb classes (the RI-pair and ZWJ rules are expressible; GB9c/Indic conjuncts are 15.1, not 15.0) or a filter function.  Generate gcb= and ExtPict first (tools/rebuild-uniprops, a one-line change to @ENUM_PROPS), then build the pattern.
docs/not-supported.md's `\X` row names this task.

=== s543p (Opus 5.5, 2026-11-27, CODE 496df8b1 = MAIN-READY-113) === Rosetta census (#2104): 1178-Reverse-a-string holds this cause (it reverses a string by its `\X` graphemes; the string holds flag pairs and a ZWJ family emoji) -- MOVED to frequency ordinary (one real program is the evidence; the subset ruling of 2026-11-24).  Silent: exit 0, nothing on stderr, a different line.
NEUTRAL REPRODUCER (run on the tree):
    binmode STDOUT, ":utf8";
    my $flags = "\x{1F1EC}\x{1F1E7}\x{1F1FA}\x{1F1F8}";              # two regional-indicator pairs
    my @c = $flags =~ /\X/g;  print scalar(@c), "\n";                # perl 2    PCL 4
    my $family = "\x{1F468}\x{200D}\x{1F469}\x{200D}\x{1F467}";     # a ZWJ sequence
    @c = $family =~ /\X/g;    print scalar(@c), "\n";                # perl 1    PCL 5
    my $acc = "e\x{301}x";
    @c = $acc =~ /\X/g;       print scalar(@c), "\n";                # both 2 (base + combining mark is right)
The program's first two lines (code-point reverse; a combining accent) are identical; only the emoji line differs.
LABEL: silent (ordinary: Rosetta 1178)

=== s543p (Opus 5.5, 2026-11-27, CODE 496df8b1) === Rosetta 1342-Split-a-character-string-based-on-change holds this cause too (it groups a string by `\X` graphemes; the regional-indicator flag splits in two).  The first differing line is the flag; the reproducer is the one above.
LABEL: silent (ordinary: Rosetta 1178, 1342)

=== s543p (Opus 5.5, 2026-11-27, CODE 496df8b1) === Rosetta 1376-String-length holds this cause too: Hangul jamo L+V+T sequences (two syllables written as six conjoining jamo) counted by `\X` -- perl 2, PCL 6.
NEUTRAL REPRODUCER (run on the tree):
    my $s = "\x{1100}\x{1161}\x{11A8}";   # one syllable as L V T
    my $n = () = $s =~ /\X/g;  print "$n\n";   # perl 1   PCL 3
LABEL: silent (ordinary: Rosetta 1178, 1342, 1376)
subject: \X is the legacy approximation (base + combining marks) since s496a, not UAX #29: a regional-indicator pair, a Hangul L+V syllable and an emoji ZWJ sequence are one cluster in perl and several in PCL
